title: Al-Layl: the giver
hookLine: the one who gives and guards himself, We ease him toward ease (92:5–7)
tomorrow: Ash-Shams: the sun and her brightness

lines: THE ONE WHO PICKS UP THE BILL.
cards: The bill lands on the table, and one friend has already paid it before anyone else has noticed. The same friend drops off soup when someone's sick, without asking whether they want soup.

For her, giving looks like breathing. For someone else at the same table, there's a tight little hesitation before handing anything over, the math running in the head. Same table, same bill, two different reflexes.
Now Al-Layl names the two directions, and makes a claim about which one gets easier with time.

teach.h: TWO PORTRAITS: GIVE, OR HOLD BACK.
teach.b: Right after the oaths, the surah draws two portraits. The first, verses five to seven: the one who gives, who is mindful of God, and who affirms what is good.

Then, in Pickthall's words: Surely We will ease his way unto the state of ease. The second, verses eight to ten, is the mirror: the one who holds back, who thinks he needs no one, and who denies the good.
For him, the way is eased toward hardship.
The words are al-yusra and al-'usra, ease and hardship, from the same two roots as the pair in Ash-Sharh a few days ago: with hardship comes ease. Here they become directions of travel.
And the verb is the same for both men: We will ease him. Both are eased. The road smooths out for each of them, just toward different places.
Giving makes giving easier; holding back makes holding back easier.

Near its end, the surah returns to the giver. Verses seventeen to twenty-one describe the one who gives his wealth to purify himself, not to repay a favor anyone did him, seeking only the face of his Lord, the Most High.
The last line of the surah is a promise: he will be content.

Some commentators report that these closing verses were revealed about Abu Bakr, who spent his money buying the freedom of enslaved believers, Bilal among them. That's a report in the tafsir, not in the text.
The text leaves the giver unnamed, so anyone can fit.

how: Many Muslims give sadaqah, voluntary charity, quietly and without being asked, alongside the obligatory zakat; the closing verses of Al-Layl are often recalled as the picture of giving for God's sake alone.

o: the sun, Surah ninety-one of the Qur'an
the night, Surah ninety-two of the Qur'an

games.q: the two portraits in Al-Layl — tap the pairs.
p: seeks only the face of his Lord

s: in Al-Layl, only the giver's road is made easy
both are eased: the giver toward ease, the one who holds back toward hardship.
the words for ease and hardship here share their roots with Ash-Sharh's
yusr and 'usr: with hardship comes ease, and here, ease and hardship as destinations.
the Qur'an names Abu Bakr in the last verses of Al-Layl
the text names no one. commentators report the verses were revealed about him.

games.q: the giver at the end of Al-Layl spends his wealth. what does the surah say he is not doing?
o: repaying a favor someone did him
seeking the face of his Lord
games.why: he isn't paying anyone back. he gives with nothing owed, seeking only his Lord, and the surah ends: he will be content.

practice: Think of the people around you this week, and let one come to mind who could use something and hasn't asked: a message, a meal, a ride, some time.
Picture giving it before they ask, and notice where the hesitation shows up in your body, if it does. Then decide what you'll give, and when.

wordCard.voice: Al-Layl. The night, Surah ninety-two: the giver is eased toward ease, and the one who holds back toward hardship. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: ease, from y-s-r, the root of yusr in Ash-Sharh; its mirror in Al-Layl is al-'usra, hardship.

carryVoice: Your line: giving makes it easy. A road smooths out the more it's walked. That's day one hundred ninety.
